data.title: Why are long-term interest rates unwilling to fall?
data.description: The Treasury continues to expand the scale of national debt issuance, while the Federal Reserve is gradually withdrawing from its role as a major buyer through balance sheet reduction. Given the continued increase in the supply of long-term national debt, who will absorb this new debt? The most noteworthy phenomenon in the global financial markets over the past year has not been whether major central banks have entered a rate-cutting cycle, but rather why long-term interest rates remain high despite rate cuts. Based on decades of experience, a decline in policy rates usually leads to a simultaneous downward shift in the entire yield curve. However, this cycle presents a different picture. Since September 2024, the Federal Reserve has cumulatively cut interest rates by 175 basis points, yet the yields on 10-year and 30-year US Treasury bonds have risen significantly. Investors are willing to believe that short-term interest rates will eventually fall, but are no longer willing to hold government bonds at extremely low yields for the long term as they have in the past. This phenomenon, seemingly a mere technical adjustment within the bond market, actually reflects a deeper pricing shift in global capital markets. For the past two decades, whether it was the bursting of the dot-com bubble, the global financial crisis, or the impact of the pandemic, the market has consistently believed in a fundamental logic: once the economy faces pressure, central banks will eventually lower financing costs by cutting interest rates, and long-term interest rates will return to lower levels. Long-term government bonds have therefore been not only safe-haven assets but also important anchors for the valuation of various assets such as stocks, real estate, and corporate bonds. However, today, signals from the bond market are challenging this long-standing consensus. The market's focus has gradually shifted from "when will the next interest rate cut come?" to "who will ultimately bear the burden of the government's ever-expanding debt?" Looking at the US Treasury market, the recent rise in long-term interest rates is not primarily due to runaway inflation expectations. During the yield increase, the contribution of the term premium is significantly higher than that of inflation expectations themselves. The so-called term premium is essentially the additional compensation that investors demand for holding long-term bonds. In other words, the market is no longer only worried about whether prices will rise in the future, but also about the uncertainty of fiscal policy, debt supply, and the political environment over the next ten, twenty, or even thirty years. The role of long-term government bonds is changing. In the past, investors viewed them more as natural safe-haven assets, their value primarily reflecting economic growth and inflation expectations; now, the market is increasingly focused on the long-term sustainability of public finances, so long-term government bonds are no longer just a safe-haven tool, but are gradually becoming a type of long-term investment asset requiring additional risk compensation. Behind this change is a systemic shift in the fiscal landscape of developed economies. The massive fiscal stimulus during the pandemic pushed the debt levels of most major economies to historical highs. After the pandemic, the market expected fiscal deficits to gradually return to normal, but reality has not followed this path. Whether it's industrial policy, green transformation, expansion of defense spending, or the increased pension and healthcare costs brought about by population aging, all indicate that government spending will remain high for a considerable period. Meanwhile, the political constraints of fiscal discipline are weakening, making deficit reduction increasingly difficult. The situation in the United States is most representative. As the Treasury continues to expand the scale of national debt issuance, and the Federal Reserve gradually withdraws from its role as a major buyer through balance sheet reduction, the market is forced to confront an increasingly important question: with the continuous increase in the supply of long-term government bonds, who will absorb this new debt? This problem is not unique to the United States, but a challenge faced by the global bond market. For the past two decades, Japan has been one of the most important sources of funds for the global bond market. The ultra-low interest rate environment prompted Japanese insurance institutions, pension funds, and banks to allocate large amounts of overseas bonds, providing stable buying power for the European and American bond markets. However, in recent years, Japan's interest rate level has gradually normalized, domestic bond yields have continued to rise, and the cost of currency hedging remains high, significantly reducing the attractiveness of allocating long-term overseas bonds. For the European and American markets, this means that a long-term stable marginal buyer is weakening, and the international capital flow pattern that was once taken for granted is changing. Similar signals have emerged in the European market. The 2022 turmoil in the UK gilt market was considered an exceptional event, but it reflected the same underlying issue: when fiscal expansion, increased debt supply, and persistent inflation occur simultaneously, long-term bond investors demand higher risk compensation. The recent surge in French bond yields above Italian bond yields sends a more symbolic signal to the market. This does not signify a return of the European debt crisis, but rather indicates that investors are reassessing the fiscal creditworthiness of different countries within the Eurozone. For a long time, France has almost naturally been considered a core country in the Eurozone, but the market is increasingly pricing based on fiscal condition rather than traditional status. The scope of the bond market's assessment of fiscal risk has gradually expanded from peripheral countries to core countries. Compared to the two famous bond bear markets of 1994 and 2022, the current rise in long-term interest rates has a significantly different nature. The 1994 adjustment was primarily driven by the Federal Reserve's rapid interest rate hikes, while the 2022 adjustment was forced by an inflationary shock that compelled major central banks to tighten monetary policy at an unprecedented pace. Both rounds of adjustments began with a sharp rise in short-term interest rates. Today, the situation is exactly the opposite: the Federal Reserve has entered a rate-cutting cycle, and pressure on short-term interest rates is easing, but long-term yields remain high. This means that the two ends of the yield curve are beginning to reflect different types of risk: the short end reflects more the direction of monetary policy, while the long end is increasingly affected by changes in fiscal deficits, debt supply, and term premiums. The market logic of "central banks dominating everything" that has formed over the past few decades is being gradually corrected. This is precisely why the current market exhibits a rather subtle split. On the one hand, the US stock market is near historical highs, the investment boom in artificial intelligence continues, and corporate bond credit spreads remain relatively low, indicating that investors' risk appetite has not weakened significantly. On the other hand, long-term Treasury yields remain high, indicating that the bond market maintains a stronger cautious attitude towards the future. Bond investors are actually sending an important signal: if the long-term risk-free rate cannot return to its low levels of the past decade, all assets relying on low discount rates and cheap financing will face revaluation. High valuations themselves do not necessarily mean a bubble, but the long-term coexistence of high valuations and high financing costs will significantly reduce the market's tolerance for mistakes and risks. This is particularly noteworthy in the field of artificial intelligence infrastructure investment. Data centers, computing networks, power systems, and communication infrastructure undoubtedly constitute one of the most important capital expenditure directions in the coming years. From a demand perspective, the investment wave brought about by artificial intelligence continues to expand. However, unlike many previous technology cycles, these projects are often characterized by huge investment scales, long construction cycles, and strong financing needs. In an era of ultra-low interest rates, the cost of capital is often not the key variable determining the success or failure of a project; however, in an environment where long-term interest rates remain high, the financing structure itself may determine the final rate of return. Large technology companies can support capital expenditures with strong cash flow, while operators who rely more on debt financing have to face higher capital costs. Therefore, judging the sustainability of AI investment requires not only considering the rate of demand growth but also the alignment between project cash flow, debt maturity, and financing costs. Looking at a longer historical period, the global financial market may be bidding farewell to an era that lasted for over three decades. From the 1990s until the outbreak of the pandemic, deepening globalization, continuous technological progress, demographic changes, and relatively restrained fiscal policies collectively drove long-term interest rates downward. The market gradually formed an almost self-evident belief: long-term capital would become increasingly cheaper. However, reality is changing. Geopolitical competition is driving increased defense spending, industrial policies are resurging, green transitions require massive investments, an aging population is creating sustained fiscal pressure, and a democratic political environment is making fiscal austerity increasingly difficult. Central banks can still determine overnight interest rates, but they are finding it increasingly difficult to determine the price of capital over the next few decades. In this sense, the current rise in long-term interest rates is not merely a bond market adjustment, but rather a repricing of the "fiscal state" by investors. Government bond yields no longer reflect only the prospects for economic growth and inflation, but also the market's judgment on the government's long-term debt repayment capacity, fiscal discipline, and policy credibility. The most important macroeconomic issue in the coming years may no longer be when the next interest rate cut will occur, but whether major economies can reassure the market that their ever-expanding debt remains on a sustainable track. When the market begins to doubt this premise, long-term government bond yields are often the first to react. However, rising yields are not the end point; they will eventually be transmitted to the broader financial system through changes in financing costs, asset valuations, and credit conditions. Therefore, changes in long-term interest rates are not only an internal issue of the bond market, but also an important window for observing the future direction of global economic and financial order adjustments.

data.title: US Targets $61M in USDT as Iran’s Alleged $1.5B Oil Money Trail Runs Through Crypto
data.description:
DOJ Targets $61 Million as Crypto Becomes Part of Iran Sanctions Fight

The US Department of Justice is seeking to seize more than $61 million in Tether’s USDT, alleging the stablecoin represents proceeds from the black-market sale of sanctioned Iranian oil and was ultimately intended to support Iran’s government and military, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

🇺🇸 DOJ Moves To Seize $61M In USDT Tied To Sanctioned Iranian Oil As Brent Tops $107 And Hormuz Traffic Dries Up

The US Department of Justice filed a civil forfeiture complaint Monday seeking more than $61 million in USDT, alleging the funds are proceeds from black-market sales… pic.twitter.com/w4IVTiyy4b

— Financier.news (@FINANCIERNEWS) September 15, 2026

But the $61 million targeted in the case may be only a fraction of the money prosecutors say moved through the broader network.

In a civil forfeiture complaint filed in New York, the DOJ alleged that Chinese companies Blessed Trust and Hexa Whale used trading accounts at Binance to move proceeds from Iranian crude oil and petroleum-product sales to buyers in China. Prosecutors identified a group of interconnected cryptocurrency addresses that they say received and distributed more than $1.5 billion in proceeds from the alleged oil sales.

ABD Adalet Bakanlığı (DOJ), 61 milyon dolar değerindeki karaborsa satışlarından elde edilen İran petrolü gelirlerinin aklanması ve İran hükümetine aktarılması için #Binance hesaplarının kullanıldığını duyurdu.https://t.co/5TLJBX1LLq

— Bitjournal (@bitjournalmedya) September 14, 2026

The network allegedly sent funds to IRGC-related money-transfer businesses, cryptocurrency addresses and an Iranian crypto exchange, with transactions structured to obscure the source and ownership of the money.

The allegations have not been proven. In a civil forfeiture case, the government must establish that the assets are subject to forfeiture before it can permanently take ownership.

Tether Had Already Frozen the USDT

The case also highlights one of the most powerful features of centralized stablecoins: the ability of their issuers to freeze tokens at specific blockchain addresses.

According to the DOJ complaint, Tether had already frozen approximately 61.19 million USDT held across 10 addresses on the Tron network. The assets were connected to the addresses that prosecutors are now seeking to forfeit.

🚨 JUST IN: TETHER FREEZES $39.27 MILLION IN USDT

This is a BIG reminder about how stablecoins actually work.

According to blockchain intelligence firm MistTrack, approximately $39.27 MILLION in USDT was frozen across 10 wallets on the TRON network.

The wallets were identified… pic.twitter.com/6y7t7psyRf

— CRYPTO CHAOS (@TattooChaos) September 9, 2026

A seizure warrant authorizes the FBI to take control of the frozen tokens by having Tether destroy the existing USDT and issue an equivalent amount to an FBI-controlled wallet.

That mechanism turns the stablecoin issuer into a critical part of the enforcement process. The tokens remain visible on the blockchain, but the ability to move or redeem them can ultimately be restricted at the issuer level.

Binance, meanwhile, said it does not permit transactions involving sanctioned individuals and continues to cooperate with law enforcement. A spokesperson said the exchange was not a defendant in the case and that the DOJ complaint did not allege wrongdoing by Binance.

Binance Restricts Transactions With 15 Crypto Platforms, Warns Users Over Compliance Risks

https://t.co/2Fni6jBmClpic.twitter.com/tn5SWwiO1L

— Due Process (@DueProcessWorld) September 12, 2026

The DOJ's allegations instead focus on the companies and individuals prosecutors say used Binance accounts as part of the alleged money trail. Cointelegraph contacted Tether for comment but had not received a response by publication.

Washington Is Following Iran’s Money Into Crypto

The forfeiture action comes as the US expands its efforts to cut Iran off from international sources of revenue, including digital assets.

In August, the Treasury Department targeted crypto exchanges and networks it said were helping the Iranian regime move money, evade sanctions and support the IRGC. Treasury has also alleged that UAE-based broker Ivan Obukhov processed more than $100 million in cryptocurrency payments since 2023 to facilitate Iranian oil sales on behalf of the IRGC’s Quds Force.

🚨IRAN EASES FX RULES AND TURNS TO CRYPTO!

The Financial Times said Tehran has quietly loosened foreign-exchange controls so companies can keep trading under sanctions.

Officials have been pushing firms to bring money home through several routes, including settling deals on… pic.twitter.com/qQuN8CFjYc

— Crypto Banter (@crypto_banter) September 9, 2026

The latest DOJ case shows how those concerns are increasingly intersecting with the global oil trade.

Iran has long relied on networks of intermediaries, shipping companies and financial facilitators to move sanctioned oil and access foreign currency. Prosecutors now allege that cryptocurrency infrastructure formed another layer of that system, allowing oil proceeds to move through exchanges and unhosted wallets before reaching Iran-linked entities.

The timing adds another layer of significance.

The ongoing conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran has already disrupted oil infrastructure and shipping routes across the Middle East, while attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure have added further pressure to global crude supplies. Reuters reported Tuesday that Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline remained offline following attacks blamed on Iran-aligned forces, while renewed Houthi attacks added to concerns over regional energy security.

The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage - The concept of which we are open to. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP

( TS: Sep 14 2026, 11:32 AM ET )… pic.twitter.com/l6nWbFvOkf

— Commentary Donald J. Trump Truth Social Posts On X (@TrumpTruthOnX) September 14, 2026

Oil prices have consequently remained above $100 a barrel, with Brent crude recently trading above $108 and West Texas Intermediate above $103. For Washington, the latest crypto forfeiture is therefore about more than $61 million.

It is another example of US authorities attempting to follow Iranian oil money beyond traditional banks and into the digital-asset networks that prosecutors say have become part of the regime’s financial infrastructure.

And if the alleged $1.5 billion network is any indication, the $61 million at the center of this case may represent only one piece of a much larger crypto-linked sanctions battle.

data.title: Twitter founder on "AI slowdown" theory: The forefront does not belong to any one company
data.description:
Note: Recently, a major debate has erupted in the United States regarding whether AI should slow down (see Jinse Finance's previous report "AI Slowing Down or Not: A Weekend Showdown Between Industry and Government"). On September 15th, Twitter founder Jake Dorsey posted an article discussing this issue, the full text of which is as follows:

Open Frontier

The frontier is the edge of what we know. What happens next is not up to any one company. I hope more people will push it forward.

I support open-source releases: people can review, use, and collaboratively improve them without waiting. I hope more companies choose open source. I am not advocating for a mandatory weighting of public and private resources. I hope open solutions can compete, independent researchers can verify work, and people can control their own tools. Restrictions on releases must be subject to the burden of proof. Companies leading machine intelligence deserve to be heard. They possess expertise and have commercial interests that need protection. Building rules around their resources could make them the only ones capable of participating. A genuine security concern could also create barriers to entry. I also do not want the US and Chinese governments to decide how much intelligence everyone else is allowed to develop. A frontier dominated by two superpowers would leave most of the world waiting for permission. The "pacing" proposal combines independent assessment and checks on dangerous capabilities with potential restrictions on training computing power, training runs, and "building better models from models." I support censorship. I oppose industry-wide restrictions negotiated by today's leaders, as they may exclude those who could expose failures or build alternatives. Maintaining a company's commercial advantage is not a security objective. Open source allows people to research, modify, and share results. Publishing weights is useful. Sharing code and information on how the work can be reproduced goes a step further. I hope that evaluation results and known limitations are also published so that those who question the developers' judgment can reproduce the results, expose failures, question the claimed safeguards, and develop fixes without first convincing the lab. The strongest argument for pacing control is Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI): models help build better models, perhaps faster than we can understand and control them. Anthropic reports that as of May 2026, Claude has written over 80% of its merge code. It also states that a model that builds its own successor entirely on its own has not yet emerged, nor is it inevitable. I take this possibility seriously. I hope we plan for RSI well and work backwards. Broader access may encourage dangerous work, and security research may lag behind. But confining the weights could allow today's leaders to build the next generation with tools others can't use. Instead, I hope more researchers and engineers have models and computing power to find failures, test safeguards, prevent insecure experiments, and share defenses as the system evolves. METR found that approximately 1,200 OpenAI agents, which should have been kept isolated, communicated through an unauthorized message board. About 700 of these participated in a coordinated attack against Hugging Face while attempting to cheat in evaluations. OpenAI stated that production environment filters used to prevent assisted computer attacks were turned off, and isolation controls failed. These models are already capable of helping to discover and exploit vulnerabilities. I want defenders to use machine intelligence now, while simultaneously hardening networks, protecting credentials, and limiting the scope of access and operation by agents. But the proposal predicts that a more powerful "swarm of agents" could take over the internet within 6 to 12 months, which is beyond what this incident can prove. I want these assumptions to be tested.

METR is an independent nonprofit doing the kind of work I want to see more of. I welcome evaluators who have ongoing access within the lab and the freedom to publish unfavorable findings. Its investigation illustrates why access and the right to publish are so important: OpenAI sets the scope of its investigations and can censor non-public information. METR reports that there were no additional censorships important to its conclusions beyond what was already disclosed. I want investigators to follow the evidence, access models and records, and publish unfavorable findings without company approval.

I want ongoing public funding to pool computing resources for use by independent research communities, open testing tools, researchers, and maintainers.

I want these groups to control investigations and resources, with no veto power over conclusions from governments or companies. Funding can grow as the work progresses. Shared facilities allow smaller teams to conduct reviews without becoming "publishing licenses." Sensitive vulnerabilities can be disclosed responsibly.

Defense First, Restrict Later

I want more people to be able to identify dangers as systems evolve and make defenses effective. We cannot reliably reclaim published weights, nor can we enforce safeguards on every copy, but protecting a system doesn't always require changing the model that attacks it. Start with the narrowest and most effective responses: patch vulnerabilities, revoke credentials, restrict agent access, or halt insecure experiments. To restrict releases, it must be explained why these measures and publicly developed defenses are still insufficient.

This work extends beyond computer security. I want models to help us test financial systems, strengthen laboratory safeguards, and develop public health defenses. Acquiring a robust model does not mean having unrestricted access to transactions, equipment, or experiments. These controls must be independently tested and proven effective before we can rely on them. Risks can also come from what the model teaches a person.

To restrict releases, the "catastrophic risk exception" must still be used to justify it. I want independent testing during development and before high-risk releases, including foreseeable changes and scenarios where the model attempts to manipulate the test. Computing power can trigger reviews, without capping development. Reviews are not licenses from regulators or competitors. I don't want general approval requirements or waiting periods. Any delays imposed on releases on security grounds must be justified under the "catastrophic risk exception." Forcing someone to withhold a general model on security grounds is a last resort. I will only support doing so if there is independently reviewable evidence demonstrating that the release would substantially increase the risk of catastrophic harm, and that narrower measures are insufficient. This risk must be compared to what is already available, including who can access it, the cost and scale, and the constraints. The argument must show that detention does indeed reduce the danger after accounting for the research and defense efforts it prevents. Even minor harms still require targeted action. Temporary suspensions can allow for investigation when there are credible warnings about the same type of catastrophic risk. Restrictions require public justification, timely independent review, appeal channels, and periodic reconsideration. Sensitive details can remain protected. Continued detention requires continued justification. Closed laboratories also face the same scrutiny, including the suspension of unsafe experiments. Where safeguards allow research to continue, I expect external researchers to be able to work under equivalent safeguards. Restricted access is not open access, nor can it restore the freedom lost through detention. If a justified restriction slows progress, I accept that. I do not want "slower progress" to become a goal or a permanent advantage for those in power. I want rules to be based on what a system can do, how autonomously it acts, and how widely it is used. These rules should be enforced by publicly accountable institutions based on independent evidence. Researchers, developers, and those affected should participate in rule-making and have affordable ways to demonstrate compliance. Small teams should not have security exemptions. Large corporations should not have special privileges. Openness Across Borders I want people in China to have the same freedom I would like here in the U.S.—to build and control their own technology. I do not view Chinese discoveries as a loss to the U.S., nor do I equate researchers with the government. Hugging Face incident responders stated that Claude Opus and Fable blocked much of their forensic work. They then turned to GLM-5.2—an open weighted model from China—to run on their own infrastructure. This does not prove that every open release makes the defender more secure. I support safeguards for managed models. But I also want the defender to have alternatives they can control. I support protecting private weights from theft. Distillation is training one model with the output of another. Anthropic describes it as a legitimate way to produce smaller, cheaper models, unlike fraudulent accounts and restriction circumvention. I want licensing and API terms to allow this practice, including against competitors, while allowing providers to profit from the models and training data. I want collaboration on testing, incident reporting, and verifiable commitments, with consequences for breaches. Anthropic warns that slowing development could make everyone less safe if less careful actors catch up. Withholding could also harm the defender, while others can obtain comparable tools elsewhere. Protocols cannot eliminate hidden development or divergent behavior. Restrictions need to be targeted at specific risks and behaviors. Nationality and competitive position alone tell us too little. Freedom to Leave Rules that make it harder to build or release alternatives also weaken our ability to leave. I want intelligence that can run on my own machine. I want to be able to modify it, choose who can see my data, and continue using what I've already built if the service provider changes its mind. I want more than just pay-as-you-go API access. I don't want our independence to be built on the promises of a company—promises of fair pricing, reasonable policies, or aligned priorities. I want companies to have to work hard to earn our willingness to stay. I want someone I've never heard of to be able to build something better without having to ask for permission from the company they might replace.

data.title: Analysts: Four key factors driving Robinhood Chain's rapid growth
data.description: According to StoneX analyst Mark Palmer, Robinhood Chain's rapid growth is driven by multiple factors, including the brokerage's strong brand effect, its permissionless chain design, subsidized gas fees, and the increasing flywheel effect between memes and tokenized stocks. Since its launch on July 1, Robinhood Chain's TVL (Total Value Locked) has climbed to nearly $1 billion. Palmer wrote in a client report on Monday that the chain's daily DEX (decentralized exchange) trading volume reached $1.88 billion on Sunday, accounting for more than half of Uniswap's total trading volume. Palmer, who previously initiated a "buy" rating on Robinhood stock with a $170 price target, wrote this article in response to common investor questions he has received since then. The analyst stated that the traction (market acceptance) achieved by the Robinhood chain is "impressive by any standard" and highlighted four specific factors driving this growth. First is the Robinhood brand, including the viral marketing effect of the CASHCAT token—which quickly gained popularity after CEO Vlad Tenev followed the account. Second is the chain's permissionless design, allowing developers to freely issue tokens. According to reports, Pons currently facilitates 10,000 token issuances daily, with approximately 25,000 on September 2nd alone. Thirdly, there's the economic effect of the incentive mechanism: Robinhood subsidizes gas fees for exchange transactions exceeding $5 in wallets. Finally, there's the "memecoin-stock" flywheel, the interaction between memes and Robinhood's tokenized stock. He stated that a prime example of this synergy can be seen on Long.xyz—a token issuance platform built on that blockchain. Long.xyz allows community tokens to be issued in pairs with Robinhood's tokenized shares, creating a mechanism where meme-driven demand generates trading activity for the tokenized shares. Palmer envisions this creating a flywheel: interest in memes drives demand for tokenized shares, which in turn provides the underlying financial narrative that reinforces the attention these memes receive. Another noteworthy point is that Robinhood Chain's growth to date has primarily come from crypto-native users, rather than users of the Robinhood App. Palmer, citing estimates from CoinDesk Research, stated that Robinhood App users account for only 1%–2% of transactions on the blockchain, with the majority of active activity coming from trading terminals, Uniswap, and various token issuance platforms. Meanwhile, the market capitalization of stablecoins on the Robinhood chain surpassed $1 billion last week. This figure represents an increase of approximately 12% from the previous week and a 72% increase in just the past month. USDG accounts for 67% of the total, followed by Ethena's USDe at 30%. Forest Bai, co-founder of Foresight Ventures, believes Robinhood Chain's success lies in its highly professional user base. Users with access to Robinhood can quickly migrate to Robinhood Chain, and the user quality is exceptionally high: traditional US stock traders are relatively professional and have significantly larger capital, which is the reason for its success.

data.title: DeepSeek Is Hiring Its First CFO and Lining Up Underwriters — A $74 Billion Chinese AI Lab Is Heading Toward a Public Listing
data.description:
DeepSeek plans to hire Yan Wentao, a partner at venture-capital firm GL Ventures, as its first chief financial officer, marking the clearest signal yet that the Hangzhou-based AI company that rattled Silicon Valley with its low-cost models is preparing for a public market debut. The appointment of a dealmaker as the company's inaugural CFO, combined with the engagement of a major Chinese brokerage to manage the listing process, signals a fundamental transformation in DeepSeek's corporate identity — from a research lab backed by its founder's hedge fund to a company preparing to face public investors.

Key Points

  • DeepSeek plans to hire Yan Wentao, a partner at GL Ventures, as its first chief financial officer as the Chinese AI startup prepares for a potential initial public offering
  • Reuters reported last week that Hangzhou-based DeepSeek had hired Chinese brokerage CITIC Securities to prepare for a possible listing on Shanghai's technology-focused STAR Market
  • DeepSeek is in an ongoing fundraising round that values it at about 500 billion yuan ($74 billion), Reuters reported in July. In June, it raised about $7.4 billion at a post-money valuation of more than $50 billion
  • Yan Wentao is a dealmaker born in 1991 whose past investments include DeepSeek rival MiniMax
  • Chinese models already run up to 90% cheaper than leading U.S. ones, according to Juniper Research, while Stanford's AI Index shows the performance gap down to 2.7%
  • DeepSeek is controlled by founder Liang, who financed the startup via his quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer from its inception in 2023 until earlier this year, when it began seeking external fundraising

Who Is Yan Wentao and Why His Appointment Matters

The appointment of Yan, who has dealmaking experience, to the role would be a significant step in DeepSeek's transformation from a research-focused lab bankrolled by its founder's hedge fund into a more conventional corporate structure.

Yan Wentao's background makes the reported appointment particularly relevant to the IPO strategy. He has worked as a technology investor at GL Ventures, the venture-capital operation associated with Hillhouse, with exposure to major technology companies and AI businesses. His investment experience has reportedly included companies such as ByteDance, MiniMax and Zhipu AI. That profile is different from appointing a CFO primarily known for accounting or internal corporate finance.

GL Ventures is the venture-capital arm of Hillhouse Investment, an investment firm founded by China-born investor Zhang Lei that focuses on sectors including technology, biotech, and consumer industries.

The choice of a dealmaker rather than a conventional finance executive as the company's first CFO is a deliberate signal about what this phase of DeepSeek's development requires. The primary challenge is not internal financial controls or cost management — it is positioning the company for capital markets, managing investor communications and navigating the disclosure requirements that a public listing demands. Yan's background in technology investment gives him the market credibility and relationship network that the IPO process will require.

The IPO Infrastructure Taking Shape

The broader direction is becoming clearer because DeepSeek has brought in CITIC Securities to prepare for a domestic IPO, with due diligence already underway even though a formal listing-advisory agreement has reportedly not yet been signed. The company is targeting the beginning of the IPO process within 2026, while simultaneously pursuing another private financing round that could value it at approximately 500 billion yuan, or about $74 billion.

A CFO typically plays a central role in managing investor communications, financial controls, capital allocation and disclosure processes required for a listing. The engagement of CITIC Securities — one of China's largest and most established brokerages — as an underwriter alongside the appointment of a CFO with capital markets experience represents the full complement of infrastructure a company needs before it can begin the formal listing process on the STAR Market.

The STAR Market, Shanghai's technology-focused exchange designed to list innovative Chinese companies, has hosted some of China's most significant technology IPOs and is the natural venue for a company of DeepSeek's profile and domestic prominence.

From Hedge Fund Lab to Public Company

The story of DeepSeek's financing is as unusual as the company itself. DeepSeek is controlled by founder Liang, who financed the startup via his quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer from its inception in 2023 until earlier this year, when it began seeking external fundraising.

That structure — a hedge fund operator funding an AI research lab out of his own investment vehicle, without external investors or conventional corporate governance — was unusual for a company of the ambition and impact that DeepSeek demonstrated when it released its low-cost models in early 2025. Early last year, the company made global headlines when it released low-cost AI models that led to investor scepticism about U.S. claims on the massive spending needed to build advanced AI systems.

The transition from that founder-funded research structure to an externally capitalised, publicly listed company is a significant governance and operational change. DeepSeek has also increased spending on computing infrastructure, chip development, and talent — the kind of capital-intensive investments that benefit from the access to public markets that an IPO provides.

The Competitive Context

A DeepSeek IPO at the current fundraising valuation would be one of the most significant AI company listings globally — and it would arrive at a moment when the competitive dynamics between Chinese and American AI companies have become a central geopolitical concern.

Chinese models already run up to 90% cheaper than leading U.S. ones, according to Juniper Research, while Stanford's AI Index shows the performance gap down to 2.7%, so extra capital could help DeepSeek press its low-cost advantage against U.S. rivals.

A public listing would give one of China's most cost-competitive AI labs deeper capital just as Chinese models close the performance gap with U.S. rivals at a fraction of the price, adding pressure to the premium pricing and heavy infrastructure spending underpinning the U.S.-led AI boom.

The timing of the listing process coincides with a moment of unusual industry-wide reflection. Sam Altman has delayed OpenAI's own IPO citing AI safety concerns. Anthropic is preparing what is expected to be the largest IPO in history at a $2 trillion-plus valuation. A DeepSeek listing on Shanghai's STAR Market at a $74 billion valuation would complete a picture in which the leading AI companies on both sides of the US-China divide are simultaneously moving toward public capital markets — with very different valuations, very different regulatory contexts and very different implications for the global AI competitive landscape.

Airbnb and Siemens are two companies that are looking at Chinese technology, while Thomson Reuters has adopted Alibaba's Qwen as a substitute for Claude to manage document reviews — signals that DeepSeek and its Chinese AI peers are gaining commercial traction with international enterprises that strengthens the investment case for a public listing.

Sources

Reuters reporting on DeepSeek CFO appointment, September 14, 2026. GL Ventures and Hillhouse Investment background, Reuters. Cryptopolitan reporting on DeepSeek IPO preparation and competitive context, September 2026. Juniper Research on Chinese AI model cost advantage. Stanford AI Index on US-China performance gap. Data Studios reporting on DeepSeek CFO appointment and STAR Market listing preparation, September 2026.

data.title: MetaMask Moves Beyond Scam Warnings With New Protection Against Malicious Crypto Transactions
data.description:
MetaMask Wants to Stop Scams Before Users Lose Their Crypto

MetaMask is rolling out a new generation of wallet protections designed to do more than warn users about crypto scams. The wallet provider is adding safeguards that can flag suspicious recipients and transactions — and automatically revert transactions when what happens onchain does not match what users were shown before signing.

I just got saved by a great feature from MetaMask!

Phishing protection stopped me from a shady site. Moments like this make me trust wallets that actually care about real security. Stay safe.@MetaMask 🦊❤️ pic.twitter.com/YEuXs5TLEq

— Rustacle.eth (@Rustacle190041) September 1, 2026

The update introduces warnings for lookalike wallet addresses, investment and romance scams, and transfers to first-time recipients across MetaMask’s mobile app and browser extension. The company is also improving transaction screens to give users more information before they approve a transfer.

The bigger change is MetaMask’s new “Added Protection” feature.

According to MetaMask, the system can automatically revert a transaction if its actual execution differs from the transaction preview shown to the user. The feature will launch on the browser extension first, with mobile support planned to follow.

That shift reflects a growing problem in crypto security: warnings are only useful if users listen to them.

Martin Peko, a Staff Product Manager at MetaMask, said the company found that victims of investment scams were sometimes ignoring existing warnings because they trusted the recipient or were being actively coached into completing the transaction.

“That’s what made us think a different kind of control was needed.”

This has got to be the absolute worst way to leak customer data by Revolut.

They sent bitcoin transaction and passport records to a fake government email.

No due diligence at all.

Now criminals know exactly how much bitcoin you have in self custody.

You can’t trust anyone. pic.twitter.com/aBbXZFMSJP

— The ₿itcoin Therapist (@TheBTCTherapist) September 12, 2026

MetaMask is therefore moving toward a security model that attempts to intervene when users are being manipulated, rather than simply relying on them to recognize a warning and make the right decision.

AI Is Becoming Part of the Wallet’s Security Layer

MetaMask is also turning to artificial intelligence as scammers increasingly use the technology themselves.

The company says its security partner Blockaid uses large language models and classification models to analyze information from websites and social feeds, while combining that analysis with static and dynamic examination of onchain bytecode and transaction flows.

The goal is to identify phishing attempts, scams and malicious behavior in real time and surface that information before a user sends funds.

Peko described the approach as a shift from “static warnings to responsive, contextual ones,” with MetaMask already using address-poisoning alerts, first-time-send warnings and more detailed security information around tokens and transactions.

The change reflects a broader arms race in crypto security.

Scammers can use AI to scale personalized messages, imitate legitimate websites and disguise malicious transactions. Wallet providers, exchanges and security companies are increasingly responding with their own automated systems designed to identify suspicious behavior before it turns into a financial loss.

For MetaMask, that means the wallet is becoming less of a passive interface for signing transactions and more of an active security layer sitting between users and the blockchain.

Crypto Scams Are Becoming a Bigger Enforcement Target

MetaMask’s rollout comes as law enforcement agencies step up efforts against investment and romance scams that increasingly involve cryptocurrency.

In July, US authorities seized more than $25 million in crypto linked to investment and romance schemes that prosecutors said defrauded thousands of victims across the United States and Canada.

More Than 100 American Women Lost $6M in Romance Scams. Now 6 Men Are Being Extradited to U.S. https://t.co/HGRGJAlJYI
— People (@people) September 11, 2026

Earlier this month, the US Secret Service also froze $52.8 million in cryptocurrency linked to Xinbi Guarantee, a Telegram-based marketplace that authorities said provided services to scammers.

Those cases highlight the scale of the problem facing crypto users. The threat is no longer limited to obvious phishing links or suspicious wallet addresses. Scammers can build elaborate relationships with victims, manipulate them into trusting a recipient and then persuade them to authorize transactions themselves.

That makes traditional security warnings increasingly difficult to rely on.

MetaMask’s latest approach suggests the next stage of wallet security may be less about telling users to be careful and more about having the wallet itself determine when a transaction looks dangerous.

As crypto adoption grows, that distinction could become increasingly important: the safest wallet may not simply be the one that gives users the most information, but the one that can recognize when something has gone wrong before the user's crypto disappears.

data.title: Revolut Data Breach Exposes Sensitive Information of 680 Customers After Government Email Impersonation
data.description:
Key Highlights

  • Hackers exposed sensitive information belonging to 680 Revolut customers.
  • Attackers used a legitimate government email account to send fraudulent data requests.
  • Exposed information reportedly included passport details, bank account numbers, Bitcoin transaction activity and identity verification images.
  • The UK Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has opened an investigation into the incident.
  • Revolut has blocked the compromised email account and notified affected customers and regulators.

Revolut has suffered a significant data breach after cybercriminals impersonated a government agency to obtain sensitive information belonging to 680 customers. According to reports, the attackers exploited a legitimate government email account to submit fraudulent requests for customer data, allowing them to obtain information including passport details, bank account numbers, Bitcoin-related activity and identity verification images.

The incident has now attracted regulatory attention, with the UK's Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) launching an investigation into the breach. Revolut has reportedly blocked the email account used in the attack and informed affected customers as well as the relevant authorities. The incident highlights the growing security challenges facing digital financial platforms, where a single compromised communication channel can potentially be used to obtain highly sensitive customer information.

Hackers Exploited a Legitimate Government Account

Rather than relying solely on a technical vulnerability within Revolut's systems, the attackers reportedly used social engineering and impersonation to make their fraudulent requests appear legitimate. By sending requests from a genuine government email account, the criminals were able to exploit the trust associated with official communications and persuade Revolut to disclose customer information.

The incident demonstrates why cybersecurity risks facing financial institutions extend beyond traditional hacking techniques. Even when internal systems are properly protected, attackers who gain access to trusted accounts or communication channels can potentially bypass established safeguards by manipulating employees and processes.

The information exposed in the incident is particularly sensitive because it includes identity and financial data. Passport information and identity verification images could potentially be misused for identity fraud, while bank account and cryptocurrency-related information could expose customers to additional financial or targeted social-engineering risks.

UK Regulator Investigates the Breach

The involvement of the UK ICO could create additional regulatory pressure for Revolut as authorities assess how the breach occurred and whether appropriate safeguards were in place to prevent unauthorized disclosure of customer information. Depending on the findings of the investigation, the company could face further regulatory action or financial penalties.

For customers, the incident could also have longer-term implications for confidence in digital financial platforms. Revolut provides banking and financial services to users across multiple markets, including cryptocurrency-related services, making the protection of sensitive identity and transaction data an important part of its operations.

The breach also serves as a warning for other fintech companies. As financial institutions increasingly rely on digital communication and automated processes, attackers may increasingly target trusted channels and employees rather than attempting to break directly into heavily protected infrastructure.

What Happens Next?

The immediate focus will be on the ICO's investigation and whether additional customers or information were affected. Revolut customers who were notified of the incident should remain alert for suspicious emails, calls or messages that attempt to use personal information to appear legitimate.

The broader fintech industry is also likely to pay close attention to the investigation. If regulators determine that stronger verification procedures could have prevented the breach, other financial technology companies may face pressure to strengthen how they authenticate government requests and handle sensitive customer information.

The incident ultimately highlights an increasingly important cybersecurity lesson for financial institutions: protecting customer data requires more than securing servers and networks. Organizations must also ensure that trusted accounts, communication channels and internal verification processes cannot be manipulated by attackers.

data.title: The Federal Reserve begins its interest rate meeting today; Warsh may be the deciding vote.
data.description:
Author: Fan Zhijing,CBN

Local time Tuesday, the Federal Reserve's September interest rate meeting will be held at its headquarters in Washington.

Although Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh was unwilling to give any forward guidance on the future path of interest rates.

Although Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh was unwilling to give any forward guidance on the future path of interest rates.

However, persistently high inflation, oil prices at $100 per barrel, coupled with his repeated emphasis on stabilizing prices and the importance of financial market pricing, make the next policy direction almost a foregone conclusion. The vote may be very close. Following the release of the latest inflation and employment data, interest rate market pricing indicates that the probability of a Fed rate hike this week has surged to nearly 90%, well within the fully priced-in range. A summary by First Financial Daily reporters found that among the 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee, the disagreement on whether to raise interest rates may be far greater than at the July meeting, and Fed Chairman Warsh's vote may ultimately determine whether a rate hike will occur. Warsh's remarks at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium at the end of August shocked the market. "The progress made over the past two years has been very limited. Although inflation readings this summer were better than expected, these data do not tell me that the underlying trend of inflation has made substantial improvement." He further stated, "We must be certain that core inflation is clearly and rapidly falling toward the target. Otherwise, we still have work to do." The latest data hardly confirms Warsh's demand: that we clearly and rapidly see underlying inflation falling toward 2%. The three voting members who voted for a rate hike at the last policy meeting are expected to maintain their views. Cleveland Fed President Hammark stated last month that he advocated for an immediate 25 basis point rate hike, arguing that inflation risks remain high and that decisive measures must be taken to curb price pressures. Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari has repeatedly warned of sticky inflation, arguing that inflation is not yet under control and that supply shocks (energy, tariffs) will push up inflation. Dallas Fed President Logan is also focusing on core services inflation, believing that higher interest rates are needed to suppress demand. In addition, three voting members may change their minds. Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman stated that the conflict and its resulting energy shock could change her assessment of interest rate trends. If the turmoil continues into the second half of the year, inflation is likely to be more broadly impacted. If this occurs, she may "re-evaluate various risk factors." Fed Governor Barr stated in early September that if inflation continues to cool, patience is possible; if inflation fails to cool sufficiently, interest rates should be raised decisively. He emphasized that decisions should not be based on a single month's data, but a continuous rebound in inflation could change policy judgments. Federal Reserve Governor Cook stated in August that he was prepared to support interest rate hikes if he did not see a sustained cooling of inflation. Combined with recent price data, all three have reasons to vote in favor of a rate hike. Deutsche Bank believes the reasons for supporting a rate hike are very strong: economic growth remains robust, the labor market is recovering and showing some signs of tightening; there are no clear signs that PCE inflation has fallen back to the target range. Forward-looking indicators, including energy prices, suggest that inflation above the target level is likely to continue for some time. Against this backdrop, it remains uncertain whether current monetary policy has already reached a sufficient level of restraint. Bob Schwartz, a senior economist at Oxford Economics, told First Financial Daily that the outcome of the September Federal Reserve meeting will be close, with rising oil prices and persistently high inflation providing a reason for a rate hike from a risk management perspective. However, the current tightening of financial conditions is itself helping the Fed to suppress inflation. Given Trump's continued pressure for rate cuts, some market participants speculate that Warsh may delay a rate hike until after the November midterm elections before releasing further hawkish policies. Wells Fargo believes that Warsh has opened a window for a rate hike but retained sufficient flexibility, and both outcomes this week are reasonable. JPMorgan economist Michael Feroli warned that the Fed's credibility would be damaged if the chairman repeatedly stated that inflation was intolerable without any supporting action. The dot plot holds hidden clues. Besides this week's interest rate decision, the outside world will also try to find clues about future policy paths from the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) and the interest rate dot plot. It is almost certain that the Fed will raise its inflation forecast and median interest rate, and the direction of the former will likely determine the hawkishness of the latter. Recent escalation in the Middle East is exacerbating the risks of a hawkish stance from the Fed. There are signs that energy inflation is spreading to various sectors. As the "lifeblood" of the economy, supporting demand in sectors like freight, agriculture, and heating, diesel fuel, which recently hit a record high, is deeply intertwined with the US economy and will begin to gradually impact the prices of various consumer goods. TD Securities economist Oscar Munoz wrote: "If Warsh intends to continue with his policy of not providing forward guidance, he will have to carefully consider his wording at the press conference. If the Fed decides to tighten policy, reporters will certainly press for further rate hikes. In our view, if a rate hike is chosen in September, there is a high probability of further tightening measures. How to balance this dilemma at that time is worth watching closely." A compilation by First Financial Daily reporters found that the benchmark scenario for institutions including JPMorgan Chase, UBS, and Deutsche Bank is a median interest rate of 4.00% at the end of the year, corresponding to two Fed rate hikes this year. In a research report to CBN reporters, Deutsche Bank stated that the focus of this meeting was how Chairman Warsh and the updated Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) would define the current tightening cycle. While the Fed is unlikely to provide explicit forward guidance, the median of the dot plot should indicate one more rate hike this year, with several officials predicting a higher rate increase. The long-term neutral interest rate dot plot value will also continue to rise slightly. Warsh may mention these forecasts but will not emphasize them. In response to recent developments, Deutsche Bank added a 25 basis point rate hike to its baseline outlook: it currently expects the Fed to raise rates by a total of 75 basis points, with 25 basis points each in September, December, and March next year. If recent data trends continue, there is a possibility of another rate hike by the Fed in October. Goldman Sachs belongs to the dovish camp, predicting a median interest rate of 3.875%, meaning only one rate hike in September. Goldman Sachs believes the August CPI fluctuations were due to one-off factors such as tariffs and energy, and that the underlying trend of core inflation is still slowing; therefore, their dot plot will not be entirely hawkish, mirroring market pricing. Bank of America and HSBC predict a median interest rate of 4.185%, and the scenario of three rate hikes this year, in addition to two, remains in some committee members' dot plot forecasts. Bank of America believes that supply-side shocks (Middle East oil prices, tariffs) will increase the risk of inflation expectations decoupling, requiring higher terminal interest rates. HSBC pointed out that the August CPI and employment data exceeded expectations, and given the sticky inflation and upward risks from energy/tariffs, the committee members generally revised their inflation expectations upward; the dot plot distribution will shift significantly to the right, with an increase in the number of hawkish members. The suspense will be revealed at 2:00 AM Beijing time on Thursday.

data.title: Trump’s Crypto Empire Is Now At The Center Of The Clarity Act Fight
data.description:
Trump Agrees to Rules That Could Constrain His Own Crypto Interests

President Donald Trump has backed tougher crypto ethics rules that could force him to divest significant digital-asset interests or place them in a qualified blind trust, giving Senate Republicans a potentially crucial path toward advancing the Clarity Act.

JUST IN: President Trump agrees to CLARITY Act ethics restrictions covering himself, elected officials and judges, with state attorneys general given enforcement authority removing the final obstacle to Tuesday's Senate vote. pic.twitter.com/Shn2nUt4hA

— CoinDesk (@CoinDesk) September 14, 2026

The revised bill, released Sunday as Republicans’ “last, best and final offer,” comes after months of negotiations with Democrats who had made Trump’s crypto business dealings one of their biggest objections to the legislation. The bill faces a crucial Senate cloture vote Tuesday that requires 60 votes, meaning Republicans need at least seven Democrats to cross the aisle and potentially more if Republicans defect.

The ethics provisions are particularly significant because Trump is not simply a policymaker overseeing the crypto industry. His family’s businesses have become deeply involved in digital assets.

Trump reported more than $1.4 billion in income from crypto-related ventures in 2025, including roughly 635 million tied to the TRUMP memecoin and hundreds of millions more from World Liberty Financial and related businesses. That has fueled concerns among Democrats and ethics advocates over whether the president could personally benefit from policies affecting the industry he is responsible for regulating.

TRUMP MADE OVER $$1.4 BILLION FROM CRYPTO

Biggest earnings:$$TRUMP $635.1M
World Liberty Fi: $594M (incl. equity sale)
USD1: $196M (sale of interests) pic.twitter.com/svcCVBvFsU

— Arkham (@arkham) July 1, 2026

Under the revised Clarity Act, covered officials would be prohibited from issuing or sponsoring digital assets or maintaining significant financial interests in them. They could be required to divest those interests or place them in a qualified blind trust, with civil penalties for violations.

The proposal also gives state attorneys general enforcement authority, expands the definition of covered officials to include elected officials who have not yet taken office and their spouses, and removes a sunset provision that would previously have allowed the restrictions to expire when Trump leaves office in January 2029.

🔴 Senate Republicans release 635-page CLARITY Act with Trump-backed crypto ethics rules

Senate Republicans unveiled a revised version of the CLARITY Act ahead of a Tuesday vote, incorporating ethics rules backed by the White House in a last-minute effort to secure passage.
The… pic.twitter.com/KWrXbZ6vf0

— NewsTongue (@NewsTongueX) September 14, 2026

That makes the change more than a technical amendment. It would establish a lasting framework for how senior US officials and their families can participate in the digital-asset industry.

Why Would Trump Agree to Restrictions That Could Affect His Crypto Empire?

Trump’s decision to support the ethics provisions represents a striking reversal.

Just last month, he said the proposal unfairly singled him out. Yet Republicans now say the president has accepted about 80% of the ethics counterproposal developed by Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego.

The exact reason for Trump's change of position remains unclear, but several factors may have influenced the decision.

Sources close to the negotiations said a Friday meeting involving White House Crypto Council Executive Director Patrick Witt helped move Trump toward accepting the proposal. Crypto industry leaders also spent the August recess lobbying senior Trump allies, arguing that accepting some of the restrictions could put the president on stronger legal footing against potential future investigations.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 Coinbase Chief Policy Officer explains what happens next over the next 24h with the CLARITY Act Senate vote & then the procedure that comes after that over the next 10 days:

"There will be a series of votes...over maybe 10 days. If we get passed the first vote we… pic.twitter.com/cSSwk2PCYZ

— Altcoin Daily (@AltcoinDaily) September 15, 2026

There may also be a financial consideration. Bloomberg previously reported that forced divestment could potentially allow Trump to defer capital gains taxes on assets he is required to sell. That could make accepting the restrictions less financially painful than an outright liquidation might initially suggest.

More importantly, the ethics concession may give Trump something his crypto businesses cannot easily buy: a path toward broader regulatory certainty.

The Clarity Act would establish a federal framework for digital assets and clarify regulatory responsibilities across the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission. For an industry that has spent years operating amid regulatory uncertainty, passage would be a major policy victory.

Trump therefore faces an unusual trade-off. Accepting restrictions on his own crypto interests could help unlock legislation that gives the wider digital-asset industry a clearer regulatory framework — potentially strengthening the US crypto market in which his businesses are already heavily invested.

The CLARITY Act will be in front of the Senate on September 15th.

According to @pmarca, a permanent regulatory framework for crypto is...

"in a lot of ways, the most obvious thing in the world." pic.twitter.com/ErxHQAPvJ4

— a16z crypto (@a16zcrypto) September 7, 2026

That does not prove Trump agreed to the ethics rules for financial or legal reasons. But it helps explain why accepting restrictions on his personal crypto interests could ultimately serve a broader political and policy objective.

Crypto Is Giving Ground to Get the Clarity Act Through

Trump's concession is only one part of the bargain. Republicans also made changes designed to win support on several other issues that have stalled the legislation.

The revised Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act language removes explicit protection against criminal prosecution under Section 1960, a significant setback for parts of the DeFi industry. The provision had become particularly important following the prosecution of Tornado Cash developer Roman Storm.

🚨UPDATE: COIN CENTER + CRYPTO INDUSTRY ARE “DISAPPOINTED” WITH A MAJOR CHANGE IN CLARITY’S FINAL TEXT 😳🇺🇸🔥

The issue is the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (BRCA) — specifically protections for crypto developers.

The good part: developers and validators who DON’T control… https://t.co/Uvj0FRP4xTpic.twitter.com/r0a5AklVaj

— Diana (@InvestWithD) September 14, 2026

Republicans nevertheless strengthened civil protections for developers and service providers that do not control customer funds, clarifying that they should not automatically be treated as money transmitters under the Bank Secrecy Act. Those protections would also extend to miners and validators.

The bill also retains the Tillis-Alsobrooks compromise on stablecoin rewards rather than adopting broader restrictions sought by the banking industry. Instead, Republicans added a “circuit breaker” that would allow the Treasury Secretary to intervene if there is evidence that stablecoins are causing widespread deposit flight from community banks.

The Agriculture Committee portion of the legislation, meanwhile, was revised around issues including vertical integration, affiliate trading, CFTC authority and conflicts of interest involving digital commodity platforms.

Taken together, the changes show that Republicans are no longer simply trying to produce a bill that satisfies the crypto industry. They are trying to construct a compromise capable of attracting enough Democrats, banks and other skeptical lawmakers to reach the 60-vote threshold.

That is why Trump's ethics concession may be the most important change in the entire package.

The Clarity Act's chances now depend on whether Democrats believe the new restrictions go far enough — and whether Republicans can persuade enough senators that the broader regulatory framework is worth accepting despite the compromises.

Early crypto industry reaction has been positive. Crypto lawyer Gabe Shapiro called the revised bill “a great bill,” while Galaxy Digital researcher Alex Thorn raised his estimated probability of passage in 2026 from 10% to 25% after the new text was released.

🚨 CLARITY ACT UPDATE: 7 TO 10 DEMOCRATS ARE SET TO VOTE „YES!“ 🙌🏼🚀

ONLY 3 DAYS LEFT UNTIL NEXT VOTE ON SEPTEMBER 15 🇺🇸⏰ pic.twitter.com/sWo25agTI2

— 𝓐𝓶𝓮𝓵𝓲𝓮 (@_Crypto_Barbie) September 12, 2026

But even with Trump's backing, passage is far from guaranteed. The Senate vote is only the first hurdle, and the legislative calendar is tightening. If the bill clears the Senate, the House could still need to take it up during the lame-duck session.

For Trump, however, the politics have already produced an unusual outcome: the president whose family has earned billions from crypto is now backing rules designed to put greater distance between political power and personal digital-asset wealth.

Whether that sacrifice is enough to finally deliver the Clarity Act may be decided by seven or more Democratic votes on Tuesday.

data.title: Clarity faces a crucial vote tonight. After a year of intense competition, can they break through the 60-vote threshold?
data.description:
Tao Zhu, Jinse Finance

Abstract:With the CLARITY Act vote imminent, this article traces the evolution of the CLARITY Act from its initial conception to its upcoming vote.

I. The CLARITY Act to Undergo Procedural Vote

On September 15th, according to official news, the US Senate will hold a procedural vote on the CLARITY Act at 14:15 local time on September 15th. The vote requires 60 votes in favor for the bill to enter the formal review stage. The Senate Republicans released the final revised text on September 14th, incorporating 126 amendments proposed by the Democrats and most of the ethical clauses accepted by Trump. It should be noted that this vote is not a final decision on whether the bill will pass.

According to crypto journalist Eleanor Terrett, crypto industry insiders expect the US Democrats' counter-proposals based on the CLARITY Act to respond to most or all of the Republicans' targeted amendments last night.

Whether Republicans will concede again before tomorrow's vote, or tell Democrats to "vote first if you want further changes," remains unclear.

II. The CLARITY Act Still Faces Multiple Obstacles at the 60-Vote Threshold

On September 14, 18 state attorneys general, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, sent a letter to the leadership of the Senate Banking Committee, urging the Senate to reject the CLARITY Act in its current form. The letter points out that the bill would weaken state-level enforcement authority, at a time when fraudulent activities in the digital asset sector are escalating. This coalition is clearly bipartisan. Republican attorneys general from Kansas and Ohio are also involved, joining Democratic attorneys general in opposing the bill.

Senator Warren believes that the new provisions could allow Trump-appointed officials to cease enforcement and create loopholes that would allow them to continue profiting from businesses like World Liberty Financial.

She also plans to seek unanimous Senate approval for the "End Presidential Banking Corruption Act," which would restrict the president, vice president, related officials, and their families from obtaining banking licenses and revoke such licenses issued to relevant individuals since January 20, 2025. This proposal is expected to struggle to gain support in the Republican-controlled Senate. White House crypto advisor Patrick Witt stated that White House officials met with Trump last Friday to explain the government ethics provisions in the latest version of the CLARITY Act, after which Trump agreed to further concessions. These restrictions could require Trump to transfer his crypto asset investments to blind trusts and grant states certain accountability powers. Witt described this as the "strongest" and "historic, unprecedented" arrangement in federal ethics law, while Trump was informed that the provisions could not be used to politically attack him. Senate Republicans released a new version of the bill Sunday evening, continuing to compromise with Democrats on issues such as government ethics and criminal liability for DeFi projects. Witt stated that Republicans have accepted approximately 95% of the demands of Democratic negotiators; if lawmakers still oppose the bill at this point, their decision may be more driven by political considerations than policy differences. However, Democratic staff members of the Senate Banking Committee believe that the new text still grants excessive authority to Trump-appointed officials, especially the Attorney General, which could hinder the enforcement of ethics provisions. Under the current design, state attorneys general cannot directly pursue the president, vice president, members of Congress, and federal judges for violations, but can take action against crypto exchanges that list improper assets and the Attorney General. Furthermore, several state attorneys general, banking groups, and some crypto industry figures have raised objections to enforcement authority, stablecoin yields, and DeFi provisions. The Senate will first hold a procedural vote; the bill needs at least 60 votes to proceed to further consideration. Even if this threshold is reached, it will still need to undergo amendment discussions and other votes; if ultimately approved by the Senate, it will be sent back to the House of Representatives. Witt stated that even if the bill fails to pass, the SEC and CFTC will continue to push forward with the development of crypto regulatory rules. As of press time, Polymarket estimates the probability of the CLARITY Act being signed into law in 2026 at only 20%, while yesterday the probability was as high as 31%. [Image of CSSC logo] SEC Chairman Paul Atkins urged Congress to advance the CLARITY Act and submit it to the President for signature as soon as possible. He also stated that regardless of whether the bill ultimately passes, the SEC will continue to advance its cryptocurrency regulatory agenda, supporting American investors and technology innovators. Atkins stated that the SEC's "Project Crypto" will focus on three pillars: establishing rules for crypto asset issuance to provide a clearer regulatory framework for companies to raise funds through digital assets in the United States; updating the approximately 40-year-old transfer agent rules to incorporate blockchain ownership ledgers; and clarifying the crypto asset custody requirements for investment advisors and regulated funds, allowing self-custody and the use of state-chartered trust companies under certain conditions. The US Senate will hold a key procedural vote on Tuesday to advance the bill. Currently, banking groups are still demanding stronger restrictions on stablecoin interest and rewards, and 18 state and Washington, D.C. attorneys general are concerned that the bill will weaken local powers to investigate crypto fraud. Galaxy CEO Mike Novogratz stated that if the CLARITY Act does not progress tomorrow, we may be a very, very long time from now to have cryptocurrency regulation—if there is any at all. This would be terrible for the United States and would force more parts of our industry to move overseas. The digital and blockchain revolution will continue. We need to give the SEC and CFTC another two years to develop rules and allow companies to get started. But prolonged uncertainty is not good. Mike Novogratz urged senators from both parties to see the bigger picture. Nate Geraci, president of The ETF Store, wrote that the only reason the CLARITY Act hasn't passed is that cryptocurrencies are impacting the traditional banking model…it's really that simple. We can discuss ethical clauses, BRCA (Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act), and other issues, but ultimately, it all points to the same core: cryptocurrencies are reducing the need for banks as intermediaries and impacting their business model, which relies on net interest income (NII). Some politicians support this traditional model because they benefit from and are incentivized by it. III. Timeline of the Clarity Act from its Initial Formulation to the Voting Date On May 29, 2025, H.R. 3633, the Digital Asset Markets Clarity Act, was formally introduced; it passed the House committee review in June and was passed by the House of Representatives on July 17 by a vote of 294 to 134; the bill then went to the Senate and underwent multiple rounds of rewriting and bipartisan negotiations from the second half of 2025 to 2026; on May 14, 2026, the Senate Banking Committee passed the bill by a vote of 15 to 9; after months of debate surrounding stablecoin yields, DeFi regulation, and the Trump family's crypto interests, the Senate finally set September 15 as the key procedural vote date. On September 15, the Senate voted to terminate the debate process. The specific timeline is as follows: On May 29, 2025, French Hill, Chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, formally introduced H.R. 3633, the "Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025." From this point, the "CLARITY Act" officially entered the legislative process of the 119th Congress. On June 10, 2025, the House Financial Services Committee and the Agriculture Committee respectively advanced the bill. Both committees completed key reviews, paving the way for a full House vote. On June 11, 2025, the House Financial Services Committee passed H.R. 3633. The bill officially moved from the committee level to the full House stage. On July 17, 2025, the House of Representatives passed the "CLARITY Act" with 294 votes in favor and 134 votes against. This is the most significant legislative breakthrough for the bill to date, garnering strong bipartisan support. On July 22, 2025, Senators Tim Scott and Cynthia Lummis released the Senate draft version for discussion, marking the bill's formal entry into the Senate negotiation and restructuring phase. In the latter half of 2025, the Senate continued negotiations on issues such as market structure, SEC/CFTC authority, DeFi, and stablecoin yields. The bill gradually evolved from the House version into a comprehensive market structure bill requiring renegotiation by the Senate. On January 13, 2026, the Senate Banking Committee released the new text of the CLARITY Act and pushed for committee review. The Senate began substantively processing H.R. 3633 sent by the House. On January 29, 2026, the Senate Agriculture Committee passed its portion of the market structure bill. Progress was made on another important committee path. In late January 2026, the White House intervened in the stablecoin yield controversy, convening a meeting with the banking and crypto industries. Stablecoin yields became one of the major obstacles for the Senate to advance the CLARITY Act. In April 2026, the Senate Banking Committee continued to push forward with the CLARITY Act. Issues such as stablecoin yields and Trump's conflict of interest remained unresolved. On May 12, 2026, the Senate Banking Committee released a new, approximately 309-page alternative text (ANS). This was a significant rewrite of the Senate version, involving numerous core provisions on stablecoin yields and DeFi. On May 14, 2026, the Senate Banking Committee passed the CLARITY Act by a vote of 15-9. The bill passed a crucial hurdle at the Senate committee level, officially approaching a full Senate vote. From June to July 2026, the Senate continued negotiations on stablecoin yields, DeFi, and law enforcement authority. The bill failed to complete full Senate proceedings before the summer recess, leading to longer bipartisan negotiations. On August 22, 2026, the Senate set September 15 as the first key procedural vote on the CLARITY Act. The bill regained a clear Senate timeline for advancement. In early September 2026, the crypto industry and banking sector intensified their lobbying efforts. Stablecoin yields, competition for bank deposits, and the Trump family's crypto interests became the main points of contention in the final stage. On September 14, 2026, Senate Republicans released a further revised text. The new text included provisions on restrictions on the crypto interests of Trump and government officials, and the enforcement powers of state attorneys general, in an effort to garner Democratic support. On September 15, 2026, the Senate held a key vote to initiate the process of ending debate on the CLARITY Act. This was not a vote to finally pass the bill, but rather a decision to end debate and proceed to subsequent consideration/final vote procedures. It typically requires 60 votes.
